primitives.name: Invariant Behavior Assumption
primitives.verbatim_quote: The assumption that under the same circumstances the same things behave in the same ways thus raises the single question of how far and in what sense the universe is really made up of such "things" which preserve an unvarying identity (mode of behavior).
primitives.assumptions: Objects exhibit consistent behavior under identical conditions; universe comprises entities with persistent identities.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When objects lack stable identity or when environmental conditions vary beyond assumed constancy.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI's probabilistic model of event likelihood based on prior knowledge of object type and context.
layer2.telemetry: Observable consistency of repeated interactions with objects across time and space.

primitives.name: Classification Dogma
primitives.verbatim_quote: It must be possible not merely to assume that the same thing will always behave in the same way, but that the same kind of thing will do the same, and that there is in fact a finite, practically manageable number of kinds of things.
primitives.assumptions: World consists of finitely many distinct kinds of objects, each exhibiting uniform behavior within its kind.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When empirical diversity exceeds cognitive capacity or when classifications become arbitrarily fine-grained.

layer2.mapping: Underpins GSE's ability to abstract complex environments into manageable state spaces using categorical equivalence classes.
layer2.telemetry: Accuracy of predictive models derived from grouped object behaviors.

primitives.name: Object Identity Theory
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is manifest that the ordinary objects of experience do not fit this description closely, certainly not such "things"as men and animals and probably not even rocks and planets in the strict sense.
primitives.assumptions: Ordinary objects cannot be treated as strictly invariant due to internal complexity and dynamic change.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At scales where internal structure or evolutionary dynamics dominate macroscopic behavior.

layer2.mapping: Relates to GSI’s need for hierarchical abstraction layers to resolve object identity at multiple granularities.
layer2.telemetry: Degree to which observed phenomena align with theoretical object models.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core tension in epistemology arises from reconciling the intuitive notion of stable 'things' with the reality of complex, evolving systems. The invariant behavior assumption posits that objects maintain consistent responses under identical conditions—a foundational premise for prediction. However, this breaks down when applied to living beings or macroscopic entities whose composition changes over time. To circumvent this, the classification dogma introduces a pragmatic solution: group similar behaviors into finite categories, enabling scalable reasoning. This leads to a duality—on one side, deterministic models grounded in fixed identities; on the other, stochastic frameworks accommodating variability. The failure mode occurs when either identity assumptions are violated or classification fails to capture essential differences among kinds. These primitives form the basis for both GSI’s Bayesian updating mechanisms and GSE’s state transition planning algorithms.
